title: What Katara Does With Anger
subtitle: Love & Duty · Chapter 20 of 40
content:
Katara did not become less angry as she got older.

She became more precise.

People who knew only the stories expected otherwise.

They remembered the healer. The girl who believed in people. The woman who could walk into a room full of frightened workers and make each one feel as if their pain mattered.

All true.

They sometimes forgot she had also crossed half the world to confront the man who murdered her mother.

They forgot hope and anger had always lived in her together.

I was reminded at a housing hearing in late autumn.

The landlord’s name was Wen Haru.

He owned six buildings in the western district and had spent two years avoiding repairs by transferring ownership between shell companies. Roofs leaked. Furnaces failed. One stairwell had partially collapsed. Complaints disappeared in the permit office because Wen Haru’s brother-in-law supervised inspections.

We had proof.

Receipts. Statements. Photographs. Medical records connecting mold exposure to respiratory illness in seventeen children.

Wen Haru arrived in silk.

He smiled at the council.

He called every tenant unfortunate.

He called every violation complicated.

He called every injury unforeseeable.

Katara sat beside me with both hands folded.

That was the first warning.

Toph sat on my other side, bare feet flat against the stone floor.

That was the second.

Aang had recused himself from the hearing because the city charter gave the Avatar emergency mediation power and he did not want that authority to contaminate an ordinary legal proceeding.

Wen Haru mistook his absence for safety.

“I have always cared deeply for my tenants,” he said.

Toph’s head turned toward me.

Lie.

I did not need her to say it.

One of the mothers in the gallery began crying quietly.

Her son had fallen through rotten floorboards two months earlier.

Wen Haru continued.

“Unfortunately, some residents have refused reasonable access for repairs.”

Katara inhaled.

I put one finger against her wrist under the table.

Not stop.

I would never tell Katara not to be angry.

Only: choose where to put it.

Her pulse hammered beneath my fingertip.

The council chair asked whether she wanted to question the witness.

Katara stood.

“Yes.”

Wen Haru smiled at her.

It disappeared within thirty seconds.

She did not shout.

She asked dates.

Exact ones.

When had he been notified about the western stairwell?

Who signed the repair order?

Why did the contractor invoice show payment for timber that never arrived?

Why had three families been threatened with eviction within forty-eight hours of filing health complaints?

Wen Haru tried charm.

Katara returned to dates.

He tried confusion.

Katara returned to names.

He tried outrage.

Katara opened the medical file.

“This child was six.”

The room changed.

Wen Haru stopped smiling.

Katara’s voice remained level.

“He fractured his pelvis because the floor of the room where he slept had rotted through.”

“That was an accident.”

“You were warned.”

“We receive many reports—”

“You were warned seven times.”

Silence.

Katara placed copies of each complaint on the table one by one.

“Seven.”

The council chair cleared her throat. “Master Katara, the documents are already in evidence.”

Katara looked at her.

The chair looked away first.

I understood, suddenly, why people described waterbending as adaptable and then made the mistake of hearing gentle.

Water could cradle.

Water could heal.

Water could also wear stone down to nothing because it had all the patience in the world.

The hearing lasted five hours.

Wen Haru lost his operating licenses before sunset.

A receivership order transferred emergency management of the buildings to the city until repairs could be completed. His brother-in-law was suspended pending investigation.

It should have felt like victory.

Instead Katara walked out of the chamber shaking.

I followed her into an empty records corridor.

She pressed both palms against the wall.

“Katara?”

“Not yet.”

I stopped.

Her shoulders rose and fell.

Water trembled inside the flask at her hip.

Not bending exactly.

Response.

After a minute she said, “I wanted to hurt him.”

The confession was so quiet I almost missed it.

I waited.

“When he called that boy an accident.” Her voice cracked. “I wanted him to be afraid.”

I moved closer but did not touch her.

“You didn’t hurt him.”

“That doesn’t make wanting it disappear.”

“No.”

Katara turned.

Tears stood in her eyes, furious tears, not soft ones.

“People act like because I chose not to take revenge once, I stopped understanding revenge.”

I thought of the stories I had heard. The Southern Raiders. Her mother. A man she had found and spared not because he deserved absolution, but because Katara refused to let murder decide who she became.

“I don’t think choosing differently means the feeling vanished.”

“No.”

She wiped her face angrily.

“I hate when people want me to be the forgiving one.”

There it was.

Not just Wen Haru.

Years of being the person who held everyone together. Years of being praised for compassion until compassion became another expectation placed on her.

“You don’t owe him forgiveness.”

Katara looked at me.

“You don’t owe anybody calm either.”

“I owe the hearing calm.”

“Maybe. Because you wanted the ruling. That’s strategy.”

Her mouth tightened.

“Not purity.”

The word hit.

Katara’s shoulders dropped.

A little.

She leaned back against the wall.

“I’m so tired of people treating anger like a failure.”

I sat on the floor.

After a second, she joined me.

The records corridor was cold. Somewhere beyond the door, clerks moved boxes and argued about seals.

“Toph likes anger,” I said.

Katara laughed wetly. “Toph likes hitting things.”

“Related field.”

“She’s going to be unbearable about this.”

“She already thinks you destroyed him.”

Katara looked over.

“How do you know?”

“She whispered ‘Sugar Queen kills with paperwork’ during the ruling.”

Katara covered her face.

Her shoulders shook.

This time with laughter.

When we got home, Aang had made dinner.

He knew about the result. News moved fast when rich men lost buildings.

He hugged Katara in the kitchen.

She held him for a long time.

Then she said into his shoulder, “I wanted to hurt him.”

Aang did not flinch.

“I know.”

Katara pulled back. “How?”

“Because I know you.”

No lecture about forgiveness.

No lesson about peace.

Aang had learned that loving Katara meant respecting moral differences he could not solve by quoting his own values at her.

He touched his forehead to hers.

“Do you want to talk about it?”

“Later.”

“Okay.”

Toph entered carrying a bottle.

“I brought victory alcohol.”

Katara stared at it. “Where did you get that?”

“Legally.”

Toph’s heartbeat, I was certain, did something interesting.

Katara pointed toward the cabinet.

“Put it away.”

Toph obeyed.

That was how worried she was.

After dinner, Katara stood in the courtyard with a basin of water.

She bent slowly.

Not combat forms.

Not healing.

Old forms from the South: circular, controlled, breath moving with the water.

Aang watched from the steps.

Toph leaned against me.

I watched Katara turn anger into motion without pretending the motion erased it.

When she finished, she came inside flushed and breathing hard.

She kissed Aang first.

Then Toph.

Then me.

Not delicate kisses.

Present ones.

“I’m still angry,” she said.

Toph grinned. “Good.”

Aang smiled. “You’re allowed.”

I touched the back of her hand.

Katara looked around our kitchen.

“Tomorrow I’m helping the tenants organize a repair committee.”

Of course she was.

That was what Katara did with anger.

She did not dissolve it into forgiveness because anger frightened other people.

She sharpened it until it could cut through lies without cutting through the person she wanted to be.

Then she used what remained to build something.

That evening, Katara took me walking along the canal.

She had spent the entire day furious and useful. I had watched her turn anger into testimony, revised procedures, and a list of names that would make several officials extremely uncomfortable.

Now, with the work finished, her hands shook.

I did not tell her to calm down.

Instead I sat beside her on the stone edge while the water moved below us.

“I wanted to break his nose,” she said.

“I know.”

“I still kind of do.”

“I know.”

She laughed once, bitter and tired.

“People act like healing means I’m supposed to be gentle all the time.”

“You froze a man to a wall once.”

She turned toward me. “Aang told you that?”

“Toph. With sound effects.”

That finally got a real laugh.

Katara leaned her shoulder into mine.

“I don’t want anger deciding who I am,” she said.

“Then don’t give it the whole job.”

She looked at me for a long moment.

“Was that advice?”

“Terrible, probably.”

“Keep trying.”

The water moved past us, never still, never harmless, carrying light from the city in broken pieces.

On the walk home, Katara did not look calmer. She looked clearer. I was starting to understand those were not the same thing, and only one of them was actually the goal.

The water kept moving. So did she. Anger came with us, but it did not get to choose the route alone.

bridge_outro: At Riverstone Terrace the next afternoon, Katara found the Lanternweald's public workshop crowded with people trying to decide how to distribute building supplies. Danse wanted a record of every piece of scrap; Greg wanted nobody turned away without a conversation. Katara listened to both and then asked the residents what they needed. Aang helped carry water. Toph inspected the footings and called three proposals 'beautifully stupid.' I watched Katara turn anger into organized care without surrendering either one. She caught my eye across the room and smiled, small and fierce. Our home could stretch across worlds, but it still had to be made in ordinary acts.
